p.title: Lobbying coalitions and their determinants: a systematic literature review

ext.title: Lobbying coalitions and their determinants: a systematic literature review
ext.document_type: Review article: systematic literature review (PRISMA-ScR scoping protocol) with a meta-analysis of tested hypotheses; no new primary data
ext.coverage: Read the full text file, all 1152 lines (front matter through references and author bios), in three chunks. Read all 59 Paul highlight annotations from the single annotation JSON. Metadata hint corrected: the hint had blank venue and DOI and a 2025 year; the text gives European Political Science Review 18 (2026), first online 5 Nov 2025, DOI 10.1017/S1755773925100143. Paul's markup is 59 Highlight annotations with empty note text. Colour clusters: yellow for most; green on p.3 (RQ1, RQ2), p.11 (minority-evidence sentences); pink on p.11 (conditions i-iii); purple on p.13 ("SNA and QCA"). Figures 1 (PRISMA flow) and 2 (trend) are images without extractable text, so their numbers come from the in-text description.
ext.research_question: RQ1: What are the key characteristics and trends of research in the academic debate on lobbying coalitions? RQ2: What are the main explanations used to account for interest groups' choice to form or join a coalition? (p. 3)
ext.theory: No single theory is adopted. The authors say the field is implicitly shaped by a rationalist framework with methodological individualism (fn. 13, p. 9). Hypotheses are sorted into macro, meso and micro levels, plus composite hypotheses. The 'weapon of the weak' argument (weaker groups pool resources; Hanegraaff and Pritoni 2019) is the central tested proposition. Interest-group definitions follow Truman (1951) and Berry (1977); coalition definitions follow Junk (2020b): policy camp, behavioral coordination, or formal organization.
ext.data: Web of Science Core Collection, English-language 'article' documents, 1 Jan 1985 to 31 Dec 2023, title/keyword search for lobby, coalition, interest, group, alliance, restricted to Political Science and Public Administration categories. Initial hits N=45; after abstract screening N=34 eligible; after snowballing N=80 final sample (unit: article). Coded by two researchers with a codebook. Meta-analysis subsample: 16 articles, 77 theoretical hypotheses (unit: hypothesis), restricted to articles that treat coalition formation as the dependent variable, use behavioral or organizational definitions, use the individual group or lobbyist as unit, and test hypotheses empirically.
ext.method: PRISMA-ScR scoping review protocol (Tricco et al. 2018) with descriptive counts (year, venue, polity, design, definitions) and a vote-count style meta-analysis: for each hypothesis, supported or not supported; confirmation rate = supported / total by level, factor and decade. Intercoder reliability by Krippendorff's alpha on 8 randomly selected articles (10% of sample): K-alpha = 0.889 (p. 4). Decade assignment uses article publication year.
ext.identification: Not applicable: descriptive literature review with no causal identification strategy. The authors frame coalition formation as the dependent variable and note that the influence-of-coalitions question is left for future work (pp. 9, 15).
ext.scope: Population: English-language articles in WoS political science and public administration journals on interest groups and lobbying coalitions, 1985-2023 (excludes sociology, economics and business journals, books, chapters and grey literature; fn. 3, 4, 17). Geography dominated by the US (41 of 80) and EU (25 of 80). Era: 1985-2023, decades 1990s, 2000s, 2010s, 2020s.

key_findings.finding: Attention to lobbying coalitions has risen slowly; at least three articles per year since 2013; peaks in 2000, 2014, 2016, 2019.
Most-receptive venues are Interest Groups & Advocacy and the Journal of European Public Policy.
key_findings.numbers: IG&A 10; JEPP 9; Journal of Politics 6; EU Politics 5; AJPS 4; APSR 4

key_findings.finding: Political systems studied are dominated by the US and EU; Canada and Australia each appear once.
key_findings.numbers: US 41; EU 25; Germany 9; Netherlands 7; UK 6; Denmark 5; Sweden 5

key_findings.finding: Large-N quantitative designs dominate; SNA is rare and QCA is absent.
key_findings.location: p. 6-7; Table 3 p. 7; Table A1 (online appendix)
key_findings.numbers: Large-N 42 of 80 (52.5%); combination of methods 12 (15.0%); qualitative case study 11 (13.8%); small-N comparison 9 (11.2%); SNA 4 (5.0%); theory only 2 (2.5%); QCA 0

key_findings.finding: Behavioral definitions of interest groups and coalitions dominate; 14 studies give no interest-group definition.
key_findings.numbers: Interest group: behavioral 56 of 80 (70%), organizational 10 (12.5%), unstated 14 (17.5%). Coalition: behavioral 59, policy camp 12, formal organization 6

key_findings.finding: Overall, 74% of tested hypotheses are supported.
Hypothesis support by level: meso best, macro worst, micro near meso.
Factor-level support: relative weakness and third-party brokers are most consistently supported; similarity and type of interest least.
key_findings.numbers: Relative weakness 11/12 (91.7%); third parties 3/3 (100%); issue context 6/7 (85.7%); ideology 6/7 (85.7%); relative strength 5/7 (71.4%); coalition features 5/7 (71.4%); external challenges 10/16 (62.5%); similarity 7/11 (63.6%); type of interest 3/5 (60%)

key_findings.finding: Weapon of the weak: most studies find weaker groups more likely to coalesce; a significant minority find the opposite; the authors suggest a minimum-resource threshold.
key_findings.numbers: Relative weakness 11 of 12 hypotheses supported; cited counter-evidence: Beyers and Donas 2014; Gray and Lowery 1998

key_findings.finding: Diachronic pattern: knowledge accumulation in the 1990s-2000s, a setback in the 2010s; macro factors abandoned after the 1990s.
Conditions for coalition formation: high-salience, conflictual issues; ideological propensity to pool resources; third-party brokers.
key_findings.numbers: No new counts; supported by the hypothesis tallies above

key_findings.finding: The effect of coalitions on influence is contradictory in the literature; not reviewed here.
key_findings.numbers: Positive: Junk 2019; Nelson and Yackee 2012. Negative: Bunea 2013; Haider-Markel 2006; Heinz et al. 1993; Junk 2020a

key_findings.finding: Future research: composite micro-meso-macro models, SNA and QCA, a possibly curvilinear resource-coalition relation, and coalitions as explanatory variables for influence.

limitations: WoS Core Collection starts in 1985; pre-1985 literature is excluded (p. 14).
Restriction to political science and public administration journals may exclude relevant work in other fields; sociology journals on nonprofits are excluded on purpose (fn. 4, fn. 17).
Books, book chapters and grey literature are excluded, which the authors say may bias the sample toward quantitative studies (fn. 3).
Snowball sampling introduces path dependence toward older, more-cited articles (fn. 5, fn. 7); more than half of the final sample came from snowballing (p. 5).
Keyword expansion (advocacy, organisation, pressure) added only 6 articles, which the authors read as validating the search terms (fn. 2).
Publication bias toward US and EU studies is acknowledged (fn. 10).
Hypothesis meta-analysis uses a dichotomy (supported or not), losing granularity about strength and limits (p. 14).
Only 16 of 80 articles enter the hypothesis analysis, and hypotheses are counted rather than weighted by study quality.
Intercoder reliability was checked on only 8 articles (10%) (p. 4).
Field fragmentation: the authors note many hypotheses and a lack of one unified framework, which may explain the mixed findings (fn. 13).

rel.summary_md:
Pritoni, Bitonti and Montalbano run a PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 80 English-language political science and public administration articles on lobbying coalitions, published 1985-2023 and indexed in Web of Science. Sixteen of those articles, contributing 77 hypotheses, enter a vote-count meta-analysis. Large-N quantitative designs dominate the field: 42 of 80 articles (52.5%). Social network analysis appears in only 4 of 80 (5%), and QCA in none. Most studies define coalitions by behavior: 59 of 80 use behavioral coordination, 12 use policy camp and 6 use formal organization. Across all 77 hypotheses, 57 are supported (74%). That figure pools US and EU studies and is UNSTRATIFIED by polity. By level, support is meso 11/14, micro 35/45 and macro 10/16. The 'weapon of the weak' hypothesis is supported in 11 of 12 tests, though a minority of studies find the reverse, and the authors suggest a minimum-resource threshold. Issue context is supported 6/7, ideology 6/7 and third-party brokers 3/3. The SNA-based tests have the weakest record of any design, 5 of 9 supported (55.6%). The review studies only why groups form coalitions. It calls the evidence on whether coalitions win contradictory and leaves that question to future work.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters because the coalitions it studies are coalitions among interest groups. Melange's 'coalitions' are mostly blocs of legislators: Ward clusters on press lean, signed partitions, and cosponsor spread. Read strictly, the review supports two narrower points about how Melange models the industries themselves. First, coalition alignment depends on the issue, which favors the per-bill contested registry over fixed global sides. Second, the CU side is modeled as a lone actor, even though the literature says weaker groups pool resources. The review gives no evidence that coalitions raise influence, so neither point justifies adding allied money as a weight.

bearings.paper_claim: Junk's (2020b) typology separates three coalition definitions: policy camp (shared positions only; 12/80 articles), behavioral coordination (59/80) and formal organization (6/80). In the reviewed literature the unit that forms a coalition is the interest group or the lobbyist, not the legislator.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 7-9; definitional counts p. 9 and p. 13
bearings.system_side: detect_coalitions runs Ward.D2 on legislators' recency-weighted graded press scores, with aggregate lean weighted x3, and labels the resulting blocs 'coalitions'. Nothing in it observes coordination. In Junk's terms it is at most a legislator 'policy camp'. The file now labels blocs pro-credit-union, hostile-to-credit-union or mixed. The brain note says all blocs are labelled pro-CU, which looks stale relative to this file.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper gives a definition only and does not validate the policy-camp reading. Its findings concern groups choosing allies, so its determinants (weakness, brokers) should not be read onto legislator blocs. If the blocs keep the name 'coalition', the label should say they are shared-position clusters with no coordination evidence.

bearings.paper_claim: Coalition formation depends on the issue. Issue-context hypotheses are supported 6/7 (85.7%). Condition (i): groups coalesce on highly salient, conflictual issues. Strange-bedfellow coalitions (Beyers and De Bruycker 2018) form issue by issue.
bearings.system_side: The registry stores an explicit counterparty set per bill, never a global one. Standard mode is the default, and admission requires owner ratification. No consumer is wired yet (CONTESTED_V1 does not exist).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence comes mostly from US and EU interest-group studies and covers whether groups form coalitions, not whether they win. It supports per-bill alignment as a structural choice. It says nothing about how large the counterparty term should be, which stays owner policy.

bearings.paper_claim: Relative weakness predicts joining a coalition (11/12 hypotheses supported, 91.7%). Weaker groups pool resources ('lobby in packs'). A significant minority of studies finds the opposite, consistent with a minimum-resource threshold.
bearings.system_side: INDUSTRY_SIDE fixes credit_union as the only 'ours' industry. Community banks, fintech, crypto, telecom and credit_arms are all 'opposition'. The registry rejects any ours-side industry, so a record has no slot for an allied industry on a bill, only for counterparties.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An ally field would be descriptive (who stood with CUs on bill X). Ally identity could come from LDA, but under D-021 co-lobbying cannot become an edge or a weight. Because the coalition-to-influence link is contradictory (p. 8), the field should not alter any score without its own validation.

bearings.paper_claim: The literature reports both positive (Junk 2019; Nelson and Yackee 2012) and negative (Bunea 2013; Haider-Markel 2006; Heinz et al. 1993; Junk 2020a) links between coalition lobbying and influence. The review leaves coalitions as an explanatory variable for influence to future work.
bearings.system_side: The pot is one PAC's budget (owner ruling of 2026-09-30), capped at PMAX $10k per member. Allies' spending is not represented, and the optimizer treats CU money as a single actor.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The weapon-of-the-weak evidence might tempt someone to pool allied industries' dollars into the CU money leg. The review does not support that, because the effect of coalitions on outcomes is unresolved. The single-actor pot remains defensible on this evidence.

gaps_exposed: Melange has no model of coalition formation among interest groups. Credit unions are a single actor, and the other industries are fixed 'opposition' in every context (build_opposition_prior.py:68-75). The literature's main determinants (relative weakness, issue salience and conflict, ideological propensity, third-party brokers) are not represented.
The contested-bills schema cannot record an allied industry on a bill, only counterparties (contested_bills.py:175-176). Strange-bedfellow alignments therefore cannot be stored.

The system has no group-to-group broker layer. Third-party brokers are the factor with the most uniform support (3/3), but no Melange component represents brokerage between interest groups. The staffer-network 'bridging' measure concerns staff layers and must not be read as brokerage or introduction access (D-025).

Several components call legislator clusters 'coalitions' (Ward blocs, signed partitions, cosponsor coalition spread). The review's definitional typology shows that none of them records coordination, so the term should be scoped wherever it is displayed.
flags: D-021: the natural way to operationalize 'behavioral coordination' coalitions from Melange data would be an industry-to-industry graph from co-registration on the same bills or issue codes in LDA. That would use LDA as an edge or weight source, which D-021 bars. LDA may only identify allies, never connect or weight them.

The paper's call for more SNA (Paul highlighted 'SNA and QCA') is not evidence that SNA works. SNA-based hypotheses have the lowest confirmation rate in Table 5: 5 of 9 (55.6%), versus 74% overall. Quote that only with its denominator. The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization), so nothing needs flagging on that front.
The 74% overall confirmation rate and the 91.7% weapon-of-the-weak rate pool US (41/80) and EU (25/80) studies. They are vote counts unweighted by study quality and should be quoted as UNSTRATIFIED.

Staleness: the component card and brain note say all Ward blocs are labelled pro-CU (a known mislabel). The current R file at cu_press_release_scraper.R:3193-3195 labels blocs as pro, hostile or mixed by mean bloc lean. Which version produced the live output is UNVERIFIED and needs a second check (DE-062).

Any pairing of this review with Melange (for example, CUs as the 'weaker' group by the joined LDA totals of ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M, vintage 2024-10-25 with coverage reliable through 2021) is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul recorded no takeaways for this paper; both annotation entries are citation-only. His highlights stress three points: SNA is underused, coalitions form around salient, conflictual issues, and third-party brokers matter. The component map attaches the paper to melange-sna.press-coalition-ward. That link merges two different coalition concepts. Pritoni reviews coalitions among interest groups, while the Ward component clusters legislators by press lean, which is at most a 'policy camp' with no coordination evidence. The paper's real implications lie elsewhere. It supports the per-bill contested registry (issue-specific alignment) and exposes a gap: the CU side is modeled as a lone actor with all other industries fixed as opposition. Paul's highlight on SNA underuse should not be taken as an endorsement of SNA. In this review SNA studies have the lowest hypothesis support rate (5/9). His note does not reflect the current bloc labels in the R code (pro, hostile and mixed now exist), and the brain card's 'all blocs pro-CU' description may also be stale.

related.why: Aref and Neal detect coalitions among House members through signed partitions, which is the legislator-level sense of 'coalition'. Pritoni covers the interest-group sense. Together they show that Melange's 'coalition' components use the legislator concept.
This is the earlier signed-partition method behind melange-sna.signed-coalitions. It works at the legislator level, so Pritoni's determinants do not transfer to it.

Kim et al.'s per-bill Support/Oppose/Engage positions from LDA reports would be the way to observe Pritoni's issue-specific group alignments, such as who stands with CUs on a given bill. D-021 still limits LDA to identity, not edges.
Romero Moreno is the stated basis for the contested-bills counterparty term. Pritoni supplies the empirical case that counterparties should be set per issue rather than globally.
Azaiez applies network (hypergraph) methods to EU lobby co-participation, which is the kind of SNA-on-group-coalitions work Pritoni says is rare (4 of 80 articles).
This is a statistical network analysis of lobbying communities, one answer to Pritoni's call for SNA of lobbying coalitions in US data.
It is cited alongside Pritoni for the same component (press-coalition-ward). It infers communities from shared text, which is again a policy-camp-style definition rather than coordination.
